summary: Describes two algorithms for IPv6, source address selection and destination address selection, giving default behavior for all implementations. They do not override choices by applications or upper layers. It was replaced by RFC 6724.

plainLanguage.summary: A computer with several addresses must choose which to use. This note gives it a sensible default ranking. It was later replaced by RFC 6724.

questions: how does ipv6 choose a source address
what is the ipv6 default policy table
does ipv6 prefer ipv6 over ipv4
subtitle: Default rules for choosing which source and destination address an IPv6 host should use.

tldr.problem: IPv6 hosts often have several source addresses and get several destination addresses from DNS, so behavior is hard to predict without common defaults.
tldr.mechanism: Two rule-based algorithms rank candidate source addresses (eight rules) and sort destination addresses (ten rules), guided by a policy table that administrators can override.
tldr.outcome: The rules give predictable default behavior for all IPv6 nodes, but RFC 3484 is obsoleted by RFC 6724.

today: RFC 3484 was a Proposed Standard published in March 2003 and is now obsoleted by RFC 6724. Use the newer RFC for current address selection rules.

sections.title: Why Default Address Selection
sections.content:
An IPv6 node can have addresses of different scopes (link-local, site-local, global), addresses that are preferred or deprecated, public and temporary addresses, and home and care-of addresses in mobile cases. Multi-homing adds still more. As a result, implementations are often faced with several possible source and destination addresses.

Dual-stack hosts must also choose between IPv6 and IPv4. A simple rule to always prefer one family can go wrong. If a name resolves to a global IPv6 address and a global IPv4 address, but the host has only a link-local IPv6 address and a global IPv4 address, IPv4 is the better choice. This RFC defines default algorithms so developers and administrators can predict behavior.

The rules MUST NOT be construed to override an application's or upper layer's explicit choice of a legal source or destination address.
sections.plainLanguage: A house with many doors needs a rule about which door to use for which visitor. This note is that rule for computer addresses.

sections.title: Context, Policy Table and Common Prefix
sections.content:
Applications typically call something like getaddrinfo() to get a list of addresses and then try them in order, while the network layer picks the source address when the application does not. So there are two algorithms: destination selection, used to sort the list that getaddrinfo() returns, and source selection, used by the IPv6 network layer.

Both share a policy table, a longest-matching-prefix lookup like a routing table. A lookup for address A gives a Precedence(A) used to sort destinations and a Label(A) used to prefer a source whose label matches the destination's. If nothing is configured, the default table SHOULD be used. Its effect is to prefer native with native, 6to4 with 6to4 and v4-compatible with v4-compatible, and to prefer IPv6 over IPv4 when matching source addresses exist.

The common prefix length, CommonPrefixLen(A, B), is the number of leading bits two addresses share, from 0 to 128.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer keeps a little scoreboard that gives each kind of address points. It also likes picking addresses that start the same way, like houses on the same street.

sections.title: Source Address Selection
sections.content:
The candidate source set is RECOMMENDED to be the unicast addresses of the outgoing interface. Anycast, multicast and the unspecified address MUST NOT be candidates. If an application names a source address that is in the candidate set, the network layer MUST respect it; if it is not, that is an error.

Otherwise eight pair-wise rules pick the best address, each acting as a tie-breaker for the previous ones:

  1. Prefer the same address as the destination.
  2. Prefer appropriate scope.
  3. Avoid deprecated addresses.
  4. Prefer home addresses.
  5. Prefer the outgoing interface.
  6. Prefer a matching label.
  7. Prefer public addresses over temporary ones.
  8. Use the longest matching prefix.

Rule 2 MUST be implemented and given high priority because it can affect interoperability. Implementations MUST give applications a way to prefer temporary over public addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: To pick which return address to write on a letter, the computer asks a list of questions in order and stops as soon as one has a clear winner.

sections.title: Destination Address Selection
sections.content:
The destination algorithm sorts a list of IPv6 and IPv4 addresses, treating IPv4 addresses as IPv4-mapped addresses when it looks them up in the policy table. It uses ten rules in order:

  1. Avoid unusable destinations.
  2. Prefer matching scope.
  3. Avoid deprecated addresses.
  4. Prefer home addresses.
  5. Prefer matching label.
  6. Prefer higher precedence.
  7. Prefer native transport over encapsulating transition mechanisms.
  8. Prefer smaller scope.
  9. Use the longest matching prefix.
  10. Otherwise leave the order unchanged.

For example, with a global IPv6 source and an IPv4 link-local source, a global IPv6 destination is tried before a global IPv4 one. With only a link-local IPv6 source and a global IPv4 source, the IPv4 destination comes first.
sections.plainLanguage: When a website has several addresses, the computer sorts them from best to worst for its own situation and tries the best first.

sections.title: Implementation and Security Notes
sections.content:
Routing is assumed to choose the outgoing interface before source selection, though source considerations may break ties between equivalent routes. If an implementation caches sorted address lists or source information, the ordering it returns should be no more than one second out of date. Rule 8 for source selection and rules 9 and 10 for destination selection may be superseded if the implementation knows better, for example which address gives the best performance.

The RFC says it has no direct impact on Internet infrastructure security. It notes a privacy concern shared by most source selection algorithms: an unfriendly node can probe a target so that it must choose source addresses for replies, and so learn correlations among the target's addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers should not rely on an old sorted list for long. Also, a sneaky visitor might learn which addresses belong to the same computer by making it reply.
